130-orthodoxy:
Gilbert K. Chesterton wrote Orthodoxy as the positive half of his earlier Heretics. The book explains, in his own words, how he personally came to believe the Christian faith. Its preface admits the task must be autobiographical to be honest.

Chapters argue from fairy tales, ethics, and paradox that orthodoxy fits the world as lived. Chesterton defends wonder, tradition, and the romance of dogma against modern philosophies. The prose is witty, combative, and quotable throughout. Orthodoxy remains a classic of Christian apologetics. Readers new to Chesterton often start here for his wit, warmth, and love of paradox.
16769-orthodoxy:
G. K. Chesterton wrote this 1908 defense of Christian faith, issued by John Lane at the Bodley Head in London. Chapters run from a defense of everything else, through the maniac and the suicide of thought, to the ethics of fairyland, the flag of the world, and the paradoxes of faith. It was reprinted many times through the 1930s.

Chesterton argues by wit and paradox, turning modern doubt back on itself with jokes, tales, and sharp turns. He holds that fairy tales teach more truth about wonder than cold systems do. The book is a lively, combative read for anyone who likes bold argument, and it remains one of his best-known works of Christian thought.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-orth:
The Feast of Orthodoxy opens Lent in the Byzantine calendar each year. It marks the defeat of Iconoclasm and the triumphant return of icons in 842. A synod at Constantinople made the anniversary a perpetual feast. The name later widened from icons to the true faith in general.

After Orthros, a procession with crosses and pictures circles around the church. The Synodikon names saints and heroes, answered three times with Eternal Memory. Heretics from Arians to Iconoclasts are then answered with Anathema. Orthodox and Uniat lists differ sharply over Photius and anti-Roman patriarchs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orthodoxy:
Orthodoxy means right belief, or purity of faith. This entry sets out what that claim involves in Catholic teaching. Right belief is not a private view, the writer insists. It is agreement with the teaching of the Church founded by Christ and led by the Holy Spirit. Divine revelation, handed to the Church as a trust for human salvation, forms both the object and the content of orthodoxy.

Scripture is cited for the stress on one faith and sound doctrine. Christ speaks of belief for salvation, and Paul charges Titus and Timothy to hold the form of sound words. The Fathers likewise urge that the deposit of revelation be kept pure and whole. Heresy, error held with obstinacy against known Church teaching, stands as the opposite pole. The entry closes by sorting the grades of error and assent.

orthodoxy:
G. K. Chesterton wrote Orthodoxy as the positive companion to his earlier Heretics, which critics had faulted for attacking modern philosophies without offering one of its own. In the preface he says the book explains not whether the Christian faith can be believed, but how he personally came to believe it. It is arranged, he warns, as a riddle and its answer, and is unavoidably autobiographical.

The chapters run from The Maniac and The Suicide of Thought through The Ethics of Elfland to The Paradoxes of Christianity and The Romance of Orthodoxy. Chesterton first sets out his solitary speculations, then shows how Christian theology suddenly satisfied them all — a repeated, surprising coincidence, he argues, that amounts to a convincing creed. The book became his best-known work of apologetics.
podcast-joerogan-k29cMrVtVXY:
British politician Rupert Lowe joins Joe Rogan for episode 2524. Lowe had just warned Tucker Carlson that British democracy was failing. He brings the same alarm to Rogan's studio.

He argues the West declines while leaders ignore voters. Rogan asks how Britain and America mirror each other. Lowe names open borders and weak parties as core faults. The talk gives American listeners a British insurgent's view in full. It suits viewers who follow populist politics on both sides of the Atlantic and want the case stated plainly. Lowe wastes no words on hope for old parties.
